description:
UK vs Germany vs Netherlands: PhD Comparison (2027)

Direct answer box (first 50 words):

The UK, Germany and the Netherlands fund PhDs in fundamentally different ways: the UK offers 3–4 year studentships on fixed stipends, Germany employs most doctoral researchers as salaried staff on TV-L E13 contracts, and the Netherlands treats every PhD as a four-year salaried employee. Which is best depends on your finances, field and plans after graduation.

The one-line summary of each system

Before the details, the biggest structural difference — and the one applicants most often misunderstand:

  • UK: You apply for a project or studentship (or self-fund). The university pays you a tax-free stipend, but you are almost never an employee. Standard duration is 3–4 years.
  • Germany: The doctorate is often a job. You are hired as a research associate (wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter) on a collective-agreement contract (usually TV-L E13, frequently at 50–75% of full time) and write your thesis alongside the work. Duration is typically 3–5 years.
  • Netherlands: Every PhD candidate at a university is a four-year employee with a fixed salary scale, pension contributions, paid holidays and usually a go/no-go assessment after the first year.

That difference shapes everything below — taxes, visa paperwork, what "funding" even means. For country-by-country stipend figures in one place, see our PhD stipend and salary comparison.

Salary details matter here: the Netherlands pays every PhD the same negotiated scale — our PhD in the Netherlands: salary and contract guide breaks down the numbers — while German pay depends on your contract percentage and state. We explain that in the TV-L E13 salary guide.

Duration and structure

UK. Three years is the classic figure, but four is now the funded norm for many studentships, and part-time doctorates stretch longer. You usually apply to a defined project or to a departmental scheme; a master's degree is commonly expected (or an integrated 1+3 route).

Germany. There is no single structure. Two paths dominate:

  1. Individual doctorate — you find a professor who agrees to supervise you (most German PhDs). Contract, funding and duration are all negotiated individually.
  2. Structured programmes — graduate schools and research training groups with coursework, cohorts and fixed funding.

Because the thesis is often written alongside a job, actual completion times run longer than the official minimum. Contracts are frequently extended in increments — a fact worth knowing before you plan.

Netherlands. Rigidly standardised: a 4-year employment contract, a first-year plan, a go/no-go review, and often a formal defence ceremony with the famous "laudatio." The predictability is a genuine advantage if you want certainty.

Two important nuances:

  • The UK stipend looks small but is tax-free, and tuition for funded students is usually paid by the funder, not you. A self-funded or scholarship-funded international PhD in the UK is a very different financial story — see the UK student visa financial requirements guide for how much you must show.
  • German and Dutch salaries carry social insurance you actually benefit from: health cover, pension credits, unemployment protection. Compare net-to-net, not gross-to-gross.

Living costs shift the picture too — London rent can erase a stipend's advantages, while German and Dutch university cities range widely. Our cost-of-living comparison for the UK, Germany and the Netherlands gives monthly budgets per city tier.

Language and admissions

  • UK: No language barrier academically. IELTS or equivalent is a formal visa/admission requirement for most international applicants.
  • Germany: Research groups in STEM routinely work in English, but admin, contracts and healthcare are German-first. Some programmes require proof of German; many don't. Funding routes like DAAD often include language support — see our DAAD scholarships guide.
  • Netherlands: English is nearly universal in academia. Dutch helps for housing, healthcare and social life, but is rarely required for the PhD itself.

Immigration policy changes frequently. Treat these as the 2026–27 picture and confirm on official government sites before making plans — start with our UK student visa and Graduate Route guide.

So which should you choose?

Choose the UK if: you want a short, English-language doctorate, you can win a fully funded studentship or a major scholarship, and you value the post-study Graduate Route window. If you need funding leads, browse the fully funded scholarships on NextApply.

Choose Germany if: you want to be paid like staff from day one, tuition-free study matters, you're in engineering/STEM where E13 contracts dominate, and you can tolerate flexible timelines. Start with our guide to studying in Germany for free.

Choose the Netherlands if: you want the most employee-like PhD — a fixed four-year contract, pension, holidays and predictable structure — and English-taught research suits you, provided you can solve the housing question early.

Frequently asked questions

Is a PhD free in Germany and the Netherlands? Yes, effectively. German public universities charge no tuition for doctoral studies (only a small semester contribution), and in the Netherlands PhD candidates are employees, so there's no tuition at all. In the UK, tuition exists — funded studentships usually cover it, self-funded students pay it.

Which country pays PhD students the most? Germany typically pays the highest gross monthly amount (E13 contracts), followed by the Netherlands' fixed scale, then the UK stipend. But UK stipends are tax-free, so compare net income and living costs rather than headline figures.

Can I do a PhD in these countries without speaking the local language? In all three, yes for the research itself — especially in STEM. The UK needs no local language at all; in Germany and the Netherlands, English-taught programmes are common, but daily life and some administrative steps are easier with the local language.

Which country is best for staying after the PhD? All three offer a post-study job-search period: around 18 months in Germany, 12 months in the Netherlands (orientation year), and the UK Graduate Route at roughly two years (longer for doctoral graduates — verify current rules, as immigration policy changes often).

Official source

Fees, salary scales and immigration rules all change annually. Always confirm current figures on the official sites: ukcisa.org.uk and gov.uk (UK), daad.de and the relevant state's TV-L tables (Germany), and werkenbij pages of Dutch universities plus ind.nl (Netherlands).
